summary: A 1969 outline for the software that would sit between a host computer and its IMP. It splits the job into a network program and a handler program, and lists questions for discussion. The original was handwritten and later retyped as a reconstruction, so it is a historical design sketch.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7 is a 1969 design outline for the software that connects a computer to the ARPANET through its IMP, the network's message machine. It proposes two programs, one to prepare the user's messages and one to drive the hardware, and lists questions the design team still had to settle. It is a planning note, not a finished specification.

questions: what is the host imp interface
what is a host heading in the arpanet
how big was an early arpanet message
subtitle: A 1969 sketch of the two programs that move a host computer's messages to and from its IMP.

tldr.problem: A host computer needs software to turn its users' send requests into messages the IMP, the network's message-handling machine, will accept, and to drive the channel hardware linking the two.
tldr.mechanism: The job is split into a Network program that multiplexes user requests, builds a 16-bit host heading and fills buffers, and a short Handler program that drives the channel hardware. They share a pool of buffers and an interface table.
tldr.outcome: It is a preliminary design outline written for discussion; it ends with open questions rather than answers, and the site text is a reconstruction of a handwritten original.

today: The unit metadata records the status of RFC 7 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a historical design sketch from May 1969, and the site text is a reconstruction of a handwritten original.

sections.title: Two Programs and Shared Tables
sections.content:
This paper is concerned with the preliminary software design of the Host-IMP interface, based on a study of BBN Report No. 763. Its purpose is both to define the functions that will be implemented and to provide a base for discussion. The system is based on two main programs: the Handler program, which drives the channel hardware unit, and the Network program, which carries out the user's transmission requests.

Because the communication is full duplex, each program can be seen as divided into an output part and an input part. The two programs exchange data through a pool of buffers and logical information through an interface table. The outline works out only the output part of each program, noting that the input part would be very similar.
sections.plainLanguage: Two helpers work together. One prepares and queues what users want to send; the other physically hands each message to the network connection. They share a small pile of storage boxes and a shared list of what is waiting.

sections.title: Preparing Outgoing Text
sections.content:
The Network program multiplexes outgoing messages and distributes incoming ones, working from the link identification numbers; a link is a logical connection between two users. When a user's program wants to send text, it supplies the text location, the text length in bytes and the destination.

From those data the Network program prepares a 16-bit host heading: 1 trace bit, 2 spare bits, an 8-bit link identification number and a 5-bit destination host. It inserts a 16-bit marking between the header and the text, made of a single one followed by fifteen zeros, so the text starts at a word boundary. It checks the text length against 1006 bytes, which is the maximum host message length of 8080 bits less the 32 bits of heading and marking, divided by 8 bits per byte. If the text is longer, the program breaks it into a sequence of messages of at most 1006 bytes each, each with its own heading; in that case a spare heading bit could mark that several messages belong to the same text. The program then transcodes EBCDIC characters to ASCII, fills the buffers and updates the interface table.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets a 16-bit label naming the link and destination, plus padding so the text starts neatly. Text longer than 1006 bytes is split into several messages, and the characters are converted from one code to another before sending.

sections.title: Handler, Buffers and Interface Table
sections.content:
The Handler program is started either by the Network program or by an I/O interrupt. It is expected to be very short, written in master mode using privileged instructions, and integrated into the operating system's I/O supervisor. It controls the channel hardware unit, starts emissions and provides data chaining between buffers, checks device status on interrupt, empties the buffers the Network program has filled, and reads and updates the interface table. It may also run a control transmission procedure with the IMP.

Buffers must be large enough to hold the maximum host message text plus its heading and marking, 1006 + 4 = 1010 bytes, so the RFC suggests a buffer size of 256 words (1024 bytes). The number of buffers would set how often a link is used. The interface table tells the Handler where the outgoing data is and how long it is; it could be a ring table with two pointers, one for filling, moved by the Network program, and one for extracting, moved by the Handler. Each entry holds a buffer address and a byte count.
sections.plainLanguage: The hardware helper is deliberately tiny and depends on a short list that says which stored message goes out next. The storage boxes are sized to fit the largest allowed message plus change.

sections.title: Open Questions
sections.content:
The outline closes with questions rather than answers. Why is there no simple control procedure between the host and the IMP? What happens if a message issued by the host reaches the IMP with a transmission error? From the BBN specifications it appears the error would be passed on to the receiving host, and the author asks whether a host-to-host control procedure is then needed.

Other questions ask where the special channel hardware unit will be connected, how the device is told that an outgoing message has ended so padding can start, and how the Handler learns the length of an incoming message. A final question asks when the Gordo documentation will be available to design the interface between user programs and the Network program.
sections.plainLanguage: The note ends with the hard questions still open: how errors should be handled, how the hardware should be wired and told when a message ends, and when more documentation would arrive.
